entries.title: Introducing the Databricks AI Index: The state of enterprise AI tokenomics
entries.summary: Developers have more AI models and coding agents to choose from than ever before....
entries.content:
A living index of real-world data on enterprise AI model adoption, spending patterns, and coding agent performance

Developers have more AI models and coding agents to choose from than ever before. Since May 2026, a new flagship proprietary or open-weight model has launched roughly every week, or every 3.7 days when regional labs are included. With so many options, knowing which models perform best, what they cost, and when to switch is becoming harder.

At Databricks, we have a unique perspective on this rapidly changing landscape. Thousands of enterprises use Unity Gateway to access and govern AI models, providing us with insights into real-world model adoption and spending. Databricks also heavily leverages AI internally across our 12,000+ employees, and we've invested substantial research in evaluating the quality and cost of new frontier models on enterprise tasks.

Today, we're launching the Databricks AI Index, a public resource that brings these insights together. Customers have repeatedly asked us how new models compare and what we're seeing across enterprise AI adoption to help inform their own investments. Now, for the first time, we're making our internal evaluation suite permanently public, with weekly updates as we evaluate new proprietary and open-weight model releases.

The Index combines two complementary sources of data:

Enterprise AI usage and spending. Aggregated, anonymized data from 10,000+ companies using Unity Gateway, spanning digital natives, Fortune 500, and Global 2000 enterprises, including traffic to external providers such as Anthropic and OpenAI. The Index tracks model adoption through token and spend shares across proprietary and open-weight models, as well as weekly AI spending patterns for individual users.

Continuously updated coding-agent evaluations. Building on the coding-agent benchmark we published in July, our latest evaluations draw on real coding-agent workflows from Databricks engineers, captured through Unity Gateway. These workflows span creating and reviewing pull requests, investigating issues, and tackling complex development tasks. Using tasks from our private codebase and withheld tests helps reduce the risk of benchmark contamination while enabling consistent comparisons of model-harness combinations and terms of task success rates and cost per completed task.

Together, these data sources show which models enterprises are adopting, how well different combinations of models and harnesses perform, and what they cost. Here are some highlights:

Enterprises are increasingly shifting workloads between model versions and providers. At mid-year, most organizations relied on a handful of Anthropic models for the majority of their work. Today, adoption is far more fragmented across model versions and providers alike. OpenAI's share of enterprise token traffic grew meaningfully over this period, driven largely by its 6 series Sol and Astra models. However, model quality continues to strongly influence provider market share; when Claude Opus 5.5 launched, momentum shifted back to Anthropic. In just six weeks, Opus 5.5 surged from 7.2% to 37.9% of proprietary-model tokens, lifting Anthropic's overall share from 57.6% to 68.8%.

The pattern of shifting workloads between models and providers aggressively matches our own AI strategy at Databricks, where we quickly evaluate and roll out new models. Two months ago, we introduced an internal Day 1 model rollout process which lets us evaluate new releases within days. This process has helped us manage cost while increasing the quality of internal AI efforts. For example, we found Opus 5.5 delivered improved quality at 29% lower cost per session than its predecessor, helping inform our decision to make it the default model for Claude Code.

Enterprises are increasingly moving beyond a single AI provider. As recent as July, approximately 64% of enterprises using Unity Gateway relied on just one model provider. By November 2, that had fallen to 28% as more organizations adopted models from more 2 or more providers.

Open-weight models are gaining ground alongside this shift. Their share of enterprise token traffic grew from 7.3% in July to 30.9% in November, more than quadrupling in less than four months. Open-weight models are also becoming increasingly competitive with proprietary alternatives. In our coding quality benchmark, three open-weight models rank among the top 10, including DeepSeek V4.1 and GLM 5.3, which both rank third with a 93.1% pass rate. In our research on open-weight models, we find that their growing capabilities, cost efficiency, and flexibility are making them an increasingly attractive option for enterprises.

Choosing the right coding agent means evaluating both the model and the harness running it. Our latest coding-agent benchmark evaluates models across nine AI labs using Claude Code and Codex. Five models from four labs (OpenAI, DeepSeek, Meta, and Anthropic) sit on the cost-quality frontier, delivering the best trade-offs between task success rates and cost.

The results show why model rankings alone don't tell the full story. Enterprises need to evaluate model and harness combinations against their own workloads, using real usage data and traces to understand the trade-offs between performance and cost.

We use this approach internally at Databricks. When evaluating whether to upgrade from Opus 4.8 to Opus 5, we analyzed the cost-quality Pareto frontier and replayed traces from our own workloads. The results showed the upgrade wasn't worth the additional cost for our use cases, so we decided to stay on 4.8.

Two models can deliver nearly the same benchmark performance at dramatically different costs. In our coding benchmark, GPT-6 Luna and Claude Opus 5.5 both achieved an 89.1% task success rate. However, Luna averaged just $0.05 per task compared with $1.62 for Opus 5.5, a roughly 32x difference.

Cost per task depends on both token prices and the amount of work a model must do to reach an answer. Extra turns, long outputs and failed attempts all increase cost. Gemini 3.8 Flash has a low token price, yet it averaged 140 turns per task and finished as one of the most expensive models in the benchmark at $11.97 per task. For coding agents, lower token prices don't guarantee lower costs when models require more work to complete a task.

Higher benchmark performance often comes at a steep price, and even small improvements in quality can carry high costs. Claude Fable 5.1 tops our benchmark with a 96.0% task success rate at $7.47 per task, while Muse Wonder scores 94.9% at just $1.53. That additional 1.1 percentage points of performance comes at nearly five times the cost. Enterprises appear to agree, and we saw Fable 5.1's share of proprietary tokens fall from 5.5% to 0.6% over 6 weeks since its launch.

The question for enterprises is how much additional quality a task actually requires. Premium models can be worth the cost for complex, high-stakes work, but less expensive alternatives may be sufficient for routine tasks. Intelligent model routing, such as Smart Routing in Unity Gateway, can help match tasks to appropriate models based on quality and cost.

AI spending varies dramatically across enterprise users. A developer running coding agents throughout the day has very different consumption patterns from those of an employee who asks an AI assistant a few questions a day. Our data highlights the stark difference: the median user spent just $2.49 on AI, while the 99th-percentile user spent $699.74, roughly 281x more.

Median weekly spending more than doubled from $1.10 over six weeks, while spending at the 90th and 99th percentile remained relatively flat. This suggests that AI consumption is growing among typical users, but a small group still accounts for most of the AI bill.

For enterprises, the trend makes visibility into the distribution of spending especially important. Understanding those differences helps organizations set more targeted budgets and spend controls without unnecessarily restricting usage.

The Databricks AI Index reveals industry-wide trends in model usage, performance, and costs. Databricks Unity Gateway helps enterprises respond to these trends across their own AI workloads:

Access and switch models without lock-in. Get centralized access to frontier, open-weight, and custom models through Databricks-hosted model serving or connections to external providers. With the Unity Gateway CLI, developers can also use approved models across supported coding harnesses such as Claude Code and Codex.

Analyze your own AI tokenomics. Use Unity Gateway usage dashboards and unified traces to understand model consumption, spending, and coding agent activity across users, teams, and applications. You can analyze and replay traces to compare model performance and costs on your own workloads, just as Databricks does internally.

Optimize model selection and costs. Use Smart Routing to match coding agent tasks to cost-effective models based on quality and performance, and apply budgets and spend caps to keep AI spending under control.

The Databricks AI Index combines aggregated, anonymized usage data from thousands of enterprises using Unity Gateway with coding agent benchmarks based on real pull requests from Databricks' private codebase. Model spending is estimated using publicly listed provider prices, and benchmark results are evaluated against hidden tests rather than an LLM judge. Results reflect the workloads and models evaluated and may vary across organizations. The current dataset covers September 21 through November 7, 2026.

Explore the Databricks AI Index to see the latest model usage trends, coding agent benchmarks, and cost comparisons. We'll continue updating the Index with the latest enterprise usage trends and coding-agent evaluations, giving developers and enterprises an ongoing resource for comparing models, performance, and cost.

Want to analyze your own AI usage, compare models, and optimize costs? Get started with the Unity Gateway quickstart guide.

The Databricks AI Index is a public resource tracking enterprise AI model adoption, spending trends, and coding agent performance. It combines aggregated, anonymized usage data from thousands of enterprises using Databricks Unity Gateway with coding agent benchmarks based on real development tasks. The Index is updated weekly as new models are evaluated.

AI models for coding should be compared on task success rate, cost per task, and performance within different coding agent harnesses. The Databricks AI Index evaluates model-harness combinations using real coding workflows from Databricks' private codebase and hidden tests to measure quality and cost. Results can vary by workload, so enterprises should also evaluate models against their own development tasks.

Lower token prices don't always translate to lower costs because models vary in how much work they need to complete a task. Models that require more reasoning turns, generate longer outputs, or make repeated attempts can consume more tokens overall. Cost per completed task is often a more useful measure of AI efficiency than token price alone.

Yes, open-weight AI models are increasingly competitive with proprietary models in coding performance and cost efficiency. In the Databricks AI Index coding benchmark, three open-weight models rank among the top 10 for task success rate, including DeepSeek V4.1 at 93.1%. The best choice depends on the workload, required quality, and cost.

Enterprises can optimize AI costs by comparing model quality and cost on their own workloads, monitoring usage, and selecting models based on task requirements. Databricks Unity Gateway provides centralized model access, usage dashboards, unified traces, and budgets to help organizations manage AI spending. Its Smart Routing capability can also match coding agent tasks to cost-effective models based on quality and performance.

entries.content:
The lakehouse category we pioneered is now a Gartner market. With Lakebase, we're building the next category for operational databases.

by Kaitlin Baumgardner, Kevin Balaji, Brianna Helm, Jonathan Keller and Susan Pierce

  • Databricks' position as a Leader in the 2026 Gartner Magic Quadrant for Data Lakehouse Platforms validates that we pioneered and established the lakehouse market category.
  • Databricks is named as the only Visionary in the Gartner Magic Quadrant for Cloud Operational Database Management Systems, a strong competitive placement that highlights our strategic vision for the future of operational databases.
  • A lakebase is a transactional database that keeps its data on the lake, in an open format, so agents can create and discard databases on demand and other engines can work with the same data. Databricks Lakebase Postgres is the first commercial implementation of this new database, and is used as the system of record for all applications: new agentic workloads, modern applications, as well as traditional transactional systems.

For decades, enterprises have run their data in two separate worlds. A warehouse or lakehouse handles analytics. Traditional OLTP databases run applications. Pipelines move data between them, creating copies, delay, and separate governance along the way.

That setup worked while dashboards and applications lived apart. AI changes that. An agent that answers a customer question, approves a transaction, or updates a forecast needs fresh operational data and deep analytical context at the same time, and it often needs to write back. Each extra pipeline adds latency, cost, and risk, so the boundary between the two systems has become a bottleneck.

These markets are evaluated largely independently. Gartner just published a Magic Quadrant for Data Lakehouse Platforms and a Magic Quadrant for Cloud Operational Database Management Systems. We see that customers, though, increasingly need the two systems to work as one.

When we introduced the lakehouse, the idea was simple. Give every data workload one open, governed foundation, instead of keeping data lakes and data warehouses as separate systems. Today thousands of organizations run data engineering, data warehousing, streaming, BI, and AI on that foundation.

We believe our position as a Leader in Gartner's first Magic Quadrant for Data Lakehouse Platforms, with the highest scores in execution, reflects what customers rely on every day:

  • AI-native. Genie lets anyone ask questions of their data in natural language, grounded in governed business semantics defined once in Unity Catalog. AI Functions run inference directly on governed data, and AI optimizes the lakehouse automatically.
  • Open by design. Data lives in open formats (Delta Lake and Apache Iceberg), so customers aren't locked into a proprietary engine.
  • Unified governance. Unity Catalog applies one set of permissions, lineage, and quality controls across data and AI.
  • Performance and cost. Serverless compute and continued engine improvements bring warehouse-class price-performance to the lakehouse.
  • Real time. Lakehouse//RT brings low-latency, high-concurrency analytics directly to lakehouse data.

We’ve seen the impact with our customers. Airwallex and Volkswagen Brasil both consolidated from Google BigQuery to Databricks Lakehouse, and have seen 3-4x faster time to insight and 25% reduced TCO respectively. Nubank, for example, runs more than 50 million queries a month with 7x better P90 query performance and more than 40% lower costs.

The lakehouse didn't begin as a category, but as a different way to build. Customers adopted it, the ecosystem built around it, and the market followed. That's the path we're on again.

The lakehouse rebuilt analytics on open, low-cost cloud storage. A lakebase does the same for operational databases. We believe it will serve as the system of record for all applications: new agentic workloads, modern applications, as well as traditional transactional systems.

In the 2026 Gartner Magic Quadrant for Cloud Operational Database Management Systems, Databricks is the only vendor named a Visionary, less than a year after Lakebase Postgres became generally available. We see that as a signal of where the category is going.

Most operational databases in use today were designed for a different era. Storage and compute are tightly coupled, so capacity is paid for at peak. Databases are heavy assets that teams seldom duplicate, and getting data to analytics or AI means building and maintaining pipelines. They weren't designed for software that agents write and run.

Lakebase Postgres starts from different assumptions. It's Postgres, so developers keep the tools they already know, but compute is separated from storage and data lives on cloud object storage, the same foundation as the lakehouse. Compute is serverless and scales to zero. Databases branch instantly, like code, so developers and agents can spin up isolated copies in seconds. And because Lakebase Postgres is native to the Databricks Data + AI Platform, its data is governed in Unity Catalog alongside everything else.

Customers are already running production workloads on a lakebase. PRADA Group uses it to serve thousands of trusted KPIs across its brands as low-latency APIs, delivering them about 130x faster (from roughly 2 seconds to 15 milliseconds) while cutting infrastructure costs by about 50%.

“Lakebase allowed us to move from traditional query-based KPI delivery to a low-latency serving layer where every metric is exposed as an API in milliseconds.”- Michele Piunti, Data Platform Manager, PRADA Group

Getting operational data into analytics has always meant copying it. A heavy analytical query can't run on the same machine as latency-sensitive transactions without causing disruptions, so teams add read replicas or build CDC pipelines into a warehouse. They pay for extra copies, wait on brittle pipelines, and end up governing two versions of the same data whose permissions drift apart. That's a big reason operational databases and analytics platforms have long been bought, run, and evaluated as separate markets.

The Lake Transactional/Analytical Processing (LTAP) architecture, enabled by the lakebase, unifies the two at the storage layer instead of forcing one engine to do both jobs. Lakebase Postgres handles transactions with full ACID guarantees, and lakehouse engines handle analytics. Both read a single durable copy of the data in open formats like Delta Lake and Apache Iceberg, governed in Unity Catalog. There's no pipeline to build and no tables to mirror, and analytical queries never slow down the application. Analytics reads instantly fresh data the application just wrote, with no delays. That's how operational and analytical data work on one foundation.

We’re already seeing customers achieving value from this unification. Posti already runs its analytics on Databricks Lakehouse, and plans to use Lakebase Postgres to power GIS and operational planning on the same governed platform, so operational applications and analytics no longer live in separate stacks.

For a deeper look at how LTAP works, read our blog post.

A few years ago, the lakehouse was an idea we had to explain. Today it's a market category, and we think the lakebase is at the start of the same shift. Applications aren't the only thing writing to databases anymore. Agents now create, branch, and query databases at a speed and scale traditional systems weren't designed for, and they need the analytical context that lives in the lakehouse.

We're building toward an open, governed foundation where every workload, operational or analytical, built by people or by agents, runs on the same data. We built the Lakehouse together with our customers, and we're building the Lakebase the same way.

entries.title: Apache Spark vs Apache Flink: which should you use?
entries.summary: For most teams, Apache Spark™ is the better choice. Spark runs batch ETL, SQL analytics,...
entries.content:
How Spark Real-Time Mode changes the streaming decision, with latency benchmarks, a feature comparison and a guide to choosing an engine.

  • Apache Spark is the default choice for most teams: one engine runs batch, SQL, machine learning and streaming, now down to millisecond latency with Real-Time Mode.
  • In a Databricks benchmark, Spark Real-Time Mode matched or beat Apache Flink on p99 latency for stateless, aggregation and join workloads.
  • Flink remains a fit for specialized cases such as very large keyed state or complex event processing on an existing Flink platform.

For most teams, Apache Spark™ is the better choice. Spark runs batch ETL, SQL analytics, machine learning and streaming on one engine, and Real-Time Mode now brings Spark streaming to millisecond, end-to-end latency. Apache Flink is a stream-native engine that fits specialized event-processing workloads, but choosing it usually means running a second engine next to Spark.

The latency gap used to be the main reason teams added Flink. With Real-Time Mode, that reason has largely gone away, and the real question becomes how many engines you want to build, operate and govern.

Spark is a unified engine for batch, streaming, SQL and AI, and Flink is a specialized stream processor. Both are open source Apache Software Foundation projects with exactly-once processing, stateful operators and SQL APIs. The difference is scope.

Spark started as a batch engine and added Structured Streaming, which treats a stream as a table that keeps growing. The same DataFrame and SQL code runs as a scheduled batch job, a micro-batch stream or a Real-Time Mode stream. Flink was designed for streaming first and treats batch as a bounded stream.

This table compares the two engines on the dimensions that usually decide the choice.

Dimension Apache Spark Apache Flink
Engine scope Unified: batch, streaming, SQL, ML and AI data prep Stream-first, with batch as a bounded stream
Streaming latency Seconds with micro-batch, milliseconds with Real-Time Mode Milliseconds
Batch and large-scale ETL Industry default for petabyte-scale batch Supported, less common in practice
Languages Python, SQL, Scala, Java, plus Go, Rust and Swift clients via Spark Connect Java, SQL, Python (PyFlink)
Stateful processing Aggregation, deduplication, joins, transformWithState, RocksDB state store Keyed state, timers, disaggregated state (ForSt) in Flink 2.x
Complex event processing Custom logic with transformWithState Built-in CEP library and SQL MATCH_RECOGNIZE
Machine learning and AI MLlib, feature pipelines, vector search in SQL, LLM data prep Limited native ML, usually paired with another system
Lakehouse integration Native Delta Lake and Apache Iceberg read and write Connectors for Iceberg and other formats
Managed options Databricks, AWS EMR and Glue, Google Cloud, Microsoft Fabric AWS, Confluent, Ververica and others

Table 1. Apache Spark and Apache Flink compared. Sources: Apache Spark Real-Time Mode docs, Apache Flink 2.0 release and Flink CEP docs.

In Databricks' published benchmark, Spark Real-Time Mode matched Flink on stateless work and had lower p99 latency on stateful aggregation and stream-static joins. The benchmark code is public, uses customer-derived feature-computation workloads and runs at 10,000 records per second for 30 minutes, measuring Kafka input-to-output latency. Databricks summarized the results as up to 92% faster than Flink.

Workload Spark Real-Time Mode p99 Apache Flink p99
Stateless transformation 3 ms 3 ms
Stateful aggregation 14 ms 45 ms
Stream-static join 9 ms 95 ms

How to read these numbers: Databricks ran the benchmark. Spark ran on Databricks and Flink ran on AWS Managed Service for Apache Flink 1.18. The results compare Spark's worst run with Flink's best run. Treat them as evidence for these workload patterns, and test your own pipeline before deciding.

Production results tell the same story. MakeMyTrip considered Flink, chose Spark Real-Time Mode to avoid a second engine and cut P50 latency to 44 ms and P99 from more than a minute to about 500 ms. Coinbase and DraftKings also run Real-Time Mode in production. For how the engine achieves this, read Breaking the microbatch barrier.

You change the trigger. Real-Time Mode is a trigger on an existing Structured Streaming query, so the same code moves between latency tiers without a rewrite.

Real-Time Mode needs update output mode and reads from and writes to Kafka or a row-level foreach sink. Stateful operators arrive in open source with Apache Spark 4.3 and are generally available on Databricks today. On Databricks, it runs on classic compute or in Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines. See the Real-Time Mode reference for the full support matrix.

REPORT

The agentic AI playbook for the enterprise

Flink can be the better fit for a small set of specialized streaming workloads. Consider it when most of these are true:

  • Very large keyed state. Flink 2.x disaggregated state is built for state far larger than local disk.
  • Complex event processing. You need pattern matching across event sequences with Flink CEP or SQL MATCH_RECOGNIZE.
  • Event-time timers on the low-latency path. Your logic depends heavily on event-time timers, which Spark Real-Time Mode does not yet support in transformWithState.
  • An existing Flink platform. You already run Flink in production and the stream doesn't feed batch, SQL or ML.

If the stream also feeds analytics, ML features or lakehouse tables, Spark avoids duplicating logic, operations and governance across two engines.

Every second engine adds a second codebase, a second skill set and a second set of governance rules. Teams that pair Spark for batch with Flink for streaming often rewrite the same business logic twice and debug drift between them.

  • One codebase. The same DataFrame and SQL logic runs as batch, micro-batch or Real-Time Mode.
  • One team. Python and SQL developers build real-time pipelines without learning a new runtime.
  • One governance model. Streaming tables and batch tables share lineage and access control in Unity Catalog.
  • One path to AI. The same pipelines build ML features for training and online inference, as DraftKings does with transformWithState.

Pipelines can also be declared instead of hand-wired. Spark Declarative Pipelines manage dependencies and incremental refresh for streaming tables.

Databricks was founded by the original creators of Apache Spark and runs Real-Time Mode as a generally available feature, including stateful operators and transformWithState. It adds Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines, Unity Catalog governance and serverless pipelines. Code written for open source Spark runs on Databricks unchanged. To get started, follow the Apache Spark tutorial: Real-Time Mode.

In Databricks' published benchmark, Spark Real-Time Mode matched Flink on stateless workloads and had lower p99 latency on stateful aggregation and stream-static joins. Results depend on the workload, so benchmark your own pipeline.

Not only. Spark Structured Streaming defaults to micro-batch, and Real-Time Mode processes records continuously with millisecond latency. You choose per query by setting the trigger.

For most workloads, no. Real-Time Mode gives Spark millisecond latency on the same engine you use for batch, SQL and ML, so you run one system instead of two.

Flink can fit specialized workloads such as very large keyed state, complex event processing or teams that already run a Flink platform for standalone streams.

Yes. Most Flink SQL and DataStream logic maps to Spark SQL and DataFrames in Structured Streaming, and Real-Time Mode covers the low-latency path. Start with stateless and aggregation jobs, then move stateful logic to transformWithState.

entries.content:
Three ways to put enterprise data and context to work with OpenAI and Databricks.

by Harish Gaur, Sully Clark, Ankith Ede and Suman Koduri

  • OpenAI brings frontier intelligence. Databricks brings enterprise data, context, and governance. Together, they help enterprises deploy AI that understands the business and can act on it.
  • Three enterprise adoption patterns: accelerating work for business users with ChatGPT and the Genie plugin, coding with enterprise-level governance through Codex and Unity Gateway, and transforming business processes with GPT models and Databricks Apps.
  • Ali Ghodsi, co-founder and CEO of Databricks, and Greg Brockman, co-founder and president of OpenAI, discussed best practices for rolling out enterprise AI

Greg Brockman, co-founder and President of OpenAI, has a simple way to describe AI without company data: “it's like hiring someone with 20 PhDs and never inviting them to a meeting.”

Enterprises want to use frontier OpenAI models on the business data they already govern in Databricks, and they want to roll AI out to far more of their employees. OpenAI and Databricks formed their partnership to make that possible. OpenAI builds the frontier models, Codex, and ChatGPT that people use every day. Databricks provides the context those tools need to work inside a company: governed data, business definitions, and access rules. Genie Ontology is the context layer in Databricks that holds those definitions and shows how the company's data fits together, so ChatGPT using Genie knows what “revenue” or “active customer” means at your company before it starts working.

Ali Ghodsi, co-founder and CEO of Databricks, and Greg Brockman, discussed the shift from chatbots to autonomous agents, and what enterprises need to get real value from them, in a conversation released earlier this week. You can watch it below.

Most companies start with OpenAI and Databricks in one of three ways:

  • Accelerate work for business users
  • Coding with enterprise-level governance,
  • Custom agents that transform business processes.

Each one is covered below.

Historically employees who needed numbers to make decisions couldn’t write SQL, so they looped in analysts or pasted data into AI tools that didn't know the company's definitions. Waiting on analysts slowed decisions down, and answers built on the wrong definitions led to the wrong decisions.

Now, they can ask these questions themselves in ChatGPT using the Databricks Genie plugin. This lets a product manager ask questions like, “How is weekly active user adoption tracking against target by plan tier?” ChatGPT will use Genie to understand the company’s metric definitions, find the relevant data, run the query in Databricks and return results back in visual graphs and charts. The plugin runs on the Genie MCP. Where once decision-making was slow, now employees can act quickly and with greater confidence in the underlying data.

Genie uses Genie Ontology, the context layer in Databricks that stores a company's approved metrics, business definitions, and how its data fits together. Genie applies the company's own definitions, so revenue in ChatGPT matches revenue in the finance reports. Users only see data they already have permission to see, and each answer links to its sources in Databricks.

Because ChatGPT has the business context from Genie Ontology, it can do more than answer. Users can ask ChatGPT Work for recommended next steps and who should be involved, share findings through Slack or email, and carry out the actions they approve through connected tools.

To get started, install the Databricks Genie plugin in ChatGPT.

AI coding agents usually spread one team at a time, and leaders lose track of who uses them, what they cost, and where code and data end up. Databricks Unity Gateway makes it easy to manage this rollout allowing a company to give OpenAI Codex to every engineer while keeping visibility and control. Developers use Codex as they do today. Codex signs in with a Databricks credential, the OpenAI key stays in the Gateway, and every request is logged. Engineering leaders set budgets, review spend by team, and pick which GPT model handles which task.

To get started, install the Unity Gateway CLI and run ug codex. The steps are in Connect Codex to Unity Gateway.

Agents that could change core business processes often stall before production, because the data they need sits behind strict security and governance rules. On Databricks, OpenAI frontier models run next to that data under Unity Catalog governance. When Databricks serves the model, there is no external API key to manage. Teams can build and evaluate agents in Agent Bricks, or write them with the OpenAI Agents SDK and deploy them as Databricks Apps.

To get started, open your Databricks workspace, go to + New > App, and choose the Agent - OpenAI Agents SDK template. The agent quickstart walks through it.

Behind the three patterns is one partnership. Here are the key facts, how the platform fits together, and the other integrations available today.

Topic Details
What it is A partnership between OpenAI and Databricks that helps enterprises use OpenAI models and tools on governed business data and context in Databricks.
When it started September 2025, as a multi-year agreement.
OpenAI products involved GPT models, Codex, ChatGPT, and the OpenAI Agents SDK.
Databricks products involved The Lakehouse, Unity Catalog, Unity Gateway, Genie, Genie Ontology, Agent Bricks, Databricks Apps, and Lakebase.
Common starting points Answers and actions for business users, coding with enterprise-level governance, and custom agents that transform business processes.
Relationship Each company is a customer of the other. OpenAI is one of Databricks' largest customers, and every Databricks engineer is getting access to Codex.
How to get started Install the Genie plugin in ChatGPT, route Codex through Unity Gateway, or deploy the OpenAI Agents SDK template in Databricks Apps.

OpenAI models, Codex, and ChatGPT connect directly to Databricks, and several Databricks products run on OpenAI models. Databricks gets early access to new OpenAI models, and OpenAI models lead on OfficeQA, a Databricks benchmark for real document work.

ChatGPT is where employees ask questions and get work done, Codex is where engineers write and review code, and Databricks Apps hosts the custom agents and apps that teams build. OpenAI frontier models do the reasoning in all three. Databricks Model Serving runs GPT models next to company data, so teams can call them from SQL, notebooks, and agents without managing a separate API key. Unity Gateway routes every model request, sets budgets by team, and keeps an audit log. The Genie plugin answers business questions in ChatGPT and Codex and gives them the business context from Genie Ontology to act on: the company's definitions, its data, and each person's access rights. The Lakehouse stores company data under Unity Catalog governance, and Lakebase, a managed Postgres database, keeps memory and state for agents.
